Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques<sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

First defined by Bouchitté and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph _G_ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of _G_. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on _P_<sub>6</sub>-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimošová, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth \(\le t\) (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013).

Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitté, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth.

Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, _i.e._ a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC- based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth \(\le t\) - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.

## 1 Introduction

The theory of potential maximal cliques (PMC) was pioneered more than twenty years ago by Bouchitté and Todinca \[3, 4, 5, 6\]. This combinatorial structure in graphs was introduced in the first place to compute efficiently the treewidth. Through the years, other applications of PMCs arose, a famous example being the design of polynomial-time algorithms for maximum weight independent set \[19, 24\]. Also, many efficient algorithms for NP-hard problems on graphs use the collection of PMCs as an input to achieve their goal, making thus the enumeration of PMCs be the bottleneck for numerous algorithmic challenges.

### 1.1 Motivations

Considering an undirected connected graph _G_=(_V,E_), a vertex set \(X\subseteq V\) is a _minimal separator_ of _G_ if there exists a pair \(a,b\in V\backslash X\) such that not only _a_ and _b_ are disconnected in _G_\\_X_ but also no proper subset of _X_ disconnects _a_ from _b_. We denote by \(\Delta_G\) the set of minimal separators of _G_. An apparently unrelated notion - but in fact with strong connections - is the concept of _potential maximal clique_ (PMC). A vertex set \(X\subseteq V\) is a PMC of _G_ if it is a maximal clique of some _minimal triangulation_ of _G_, _i.e._ an inclusion-wise minimal add-on of edges to make _G_ become chordal. Let \(\Pi_G\) denote the set of all PMCs of _G_. Concretely, due to the strong relationship between triangulations and tree decompositions, PMCs can be seen as "candidates for bags of useful tree decompositions", echoing the words of Grzesik, Klimosov, Pilipczuk and Pilipczuk in \[19\]. This reason explains why PMCs play a crucial role in the design of exact exponential-time algorithms, as detailed below. Note that PMCs can be defined for disconnected graphs, but since the set of PMCs of a disconnected graph is simply the disjoint union of PMCs of its connected components, all graphs considered in this paper are connected.

We call Treewidth the problem of determining the treewidth of a graph. Coming back to the analogy between PMCs and bags of tree decompositions, computing the set \(\Pi_G\) seems to be a natural approach to obtain the treewidth of _G_ and/or an optimal tree decomposition. This is what Bouchitté and Todinca stated formally in \[5\]. They proposed a dynamic programming procedure which solves Treewidth in time \(O(n^2\cdot|\Delta_G|\cdot|\Pi_G|)\), given that the sets \(\Delta_G\) and \(\Pi_G\) are provided, with _n_=|_V_|. This was later improved \[12\] with a running time \(O(n^3|\Pi_G|)\). Such execution times are exponential since a graph may admit a number of minimal separators and/or PMCs exponential in _n_.

In these aforementioned algorithms for Treewidth, PMCs are essential to achieve the divide-and-conquer scheme which determines the treewidth of successive graphs until going up to the input one. However, if we aim at using such algorithms in practice, we must be able to enumerate PMCs before the execution, as efficiently as possible. Minimal separators of a graph _G_ can be enumerated in polynomial delay \[1\], which implies a global enumeration time of \(O(n^3|\Delta_G|)\), which is output-linear. Bouchitté and Todinca \[6\] proposed an algorithm (that we call BT-enum) enumerating all PMCs of a graph with a running time in \(O(n^2m|\Delta_G|^2)\), where _m_=|_E_|. Additionally, they established the following inequality which strengthens even more the links between minimal separators and PMCs: \(\frac{|\Delta_G|}{n}\le|\Pi_G|\le n|\Delta_G|^2+n|\Delta_G|+1\). Due to the left-hand side of this inequality, their algorithm BT-enum guarantees an output-quadratic time: there can be instances on which the time taken by the enumeration is quadratic in the size of the output \(\Pi_G\). Thanks to BT-enum, by assembling results together, Treewidth<tbc>

<tbc>can be solved in time \(O(n^2m|\Delta_G|^2+n^3|\Pi_G|)=O(n^4|\Delta_G|^2)\), which can be quadratic in the number of PMCs (if we neglect polynomial factors).

An important challenge consists thus in identifying efficient algorithms for the enumeration of PMCs. Since BT-enum is output-quadratic, a natural question is whether an output-linear time PMC enumeration algorithm can be built. This question is part of the list of open problems in parameterized and exact computations at IPEC 2006 conference \[2\], and was also stated in several articles \[12, 18, 21, 23, 29\] as a way to obtain a faster exponential time algorithm for Treewidth. Indeed, a PMC enumeration algorithm running in \(O(n^{O(1)}|\Pi_G|)=\tilde{O}(|\Pi_G|)^1\) would imply the same time complexity for Treewidth, improving the current \(\tilde{O}(|\Delta_G|^2)\), especially on graphs where values \(|\Delta_G|\) and \(|\Pi_G|\) are close. In this paper, we answer positively to this open question.

A bunch of results on PMCs deals with their number in function of _n_. Fomin and Villanger presented the two most recent ones. In the first one \[15\], they prove that \(|\Pi_G|=O(1.7549^n)\) and, moreover, the list \(\Pi_G\) can be computed in time _O_(1.7549_<sup>n</sup>_), matching tightly this upper bound. In the second one \[16\], they establish exactly the same contributions, but with the new bound _O_(1.7346_<sup>n</sup>_). Since the computation of PMCs is the bottleneck for Treewidth, this latter result offers the possibility to solve it in exponential time _O_(1.7346_<sup>n</sup>_). This is, to the best of our knowledge, the lower running time for Treewidth if we look at exact exponential-time algorithms, function of _n_. Unfortunately, this enumeration algorithm for PMCs admits some limits in practice, since it may take time \(\Theta(1.7346^n)\) while the size of \(\Pi_G\) is much smaller. Moreover, this bound is probably not tight. For these reasons, the importance of designing an output-linear time algorithm for PMC enumeration is reinforced.

While Fomin and Villanger studied deeply the enumeration of PMCs through extremal combinatorics, they also identified other applications \[12, 15, 16\]. One of their interesting results follows \[16\]. Given a graph _G_, an integer \(t\ge 0\), and sets \(\Delta_G\) and \(\Pi_G\), one can compute the largest induced subgraph of treewidth at most _t_ in time \(O(n^{O(t)}(|\Pi_G|+|\Delta_G|))\). We call this problem \(\text{lis-}(\text{tw}\le t)\). Since enumerating PMCs can be done in time \(O(n^2m|\Delta_G|^2)\) as written above, this result can be restated as function of the input graph only. Given a graph _G_ and an integer \(t\ge 0\), \(\text{lis-}(\text{tw}\le t)\) can be solved in time \(O(n^{O(t)}|\Delta_G|^2)\). Again, our main contribution to PMC enumeration will allow us to improve this statement.

Furthermore, a few years later, this result was generalized to a larger set of problems in \[14\]. In fact, given a graph _G_ and its set of PMCs \(\Pi_G\), an integer \(t\ge 0\), and a CMSO<sup>2</sup> formula \(\varphi\), one can compute in time \(O(n^{O(t)}\cdot f(t,\varphi)\cdot|\Pi_G|)\) the largest set of vertices \(X\subseteq F\) such that _F_ has treewidth at most _t_ and \((G[F],X)\vDash\varphi\), where _f_ is some exponential function. Behind this rather abstract formulation - let us call it \(\text{max-}(\text{tw}\le t,\varphi)\) - we can find many problems, classical ones as Maximum Independent Set and Maximum Induced Forest and more exotic ones as Independent Cycle Packing and Maximum Induced Subgraph with \(\le\ell\) copies of _p_-cycles.

In 2014, a major algorithmic impact of PMCs came with the design of a polynomial-time algorithm for Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) on _P_<sub>5</sub>-free graphs by Lokshtanov, Vatshelle and Villanger \[24\]. The algorithm consists in two steps: first the computation of a polynomial-size family F of particular PMCs, second a dynamic programming procedure based on F to retrieve the maximum-weighted independent set. Inspired by this technique,<tbc>

the authors of \[19\] proposed a polynomial-time algorithm for MWIS on _P_<sub>6</sub>-free graphs. This breakthrough strengthened the general belief that MWIS is polynomial-time solvable on _P<sub>k</sub>_- free graphs, for any constant _k_. Very recently, the authors of \[9\] designed a similar technique to tackle \(\mathrm{max}\)-(\(\mathrm{tw}\le t,\varphi\)) on _P_<sub>6</sub>-free graphs in polynomial-time for constant _t_. Furthermore, _K_<sub>2_,q_</sub>-induced-minor-free graphs were characterized thanks to PMCs, enabling MWIS to be solved in polynomial time in this graph class \[11\].

Another application of PMCs is the study of the Minimum fill-in problem: can a graph _G_ become chordal with the add-on of at most _k_ edges? This question is naturally related to PMCs as it deals with triangulations. As for Treewidth, Bouchitté and Todinca \[5\] proved that, given a graph _G_ with its lists of minimal separators \(\Delta_G\) and PMCs \(\Pi_G\), we can solve Minimum fill-in in time \(O(n^2\cdot|\Delta_G|\cdot|\Pi_G|)\). This was later improved \[12\] with a running time \(O(n^3|\Pi_G|)\), depending only on list \(\Pi_G\). Again, PMC enumeration stands as a bottleneck for solving Minimum fill-in. From a parameterized point of view, an exact subexponential parameterized algorithm was proposed \[17\], with a running time \(O(2^{O(\sqrt{k}\mathrm{log}k)}+k^2nm)\). It enumerates, as a subroutine, a list of certain PMCs called _vital_ PMCs.

From a more practical viewpoint, Korhonen presented a few years ago an experimental study of the enumeration algorithms based on PMCs in \[21\]. It confirmed that going through PMC enumeration is among the most effective methods to solve Treewidth, outperforming declarative approaches. Furthermore, the PMC-based algorithm evoked earlier for Minimum fill-in obtains the best performance on benchmarks, defeating integer-programming alternatives. The latter conclusion also holds for PMC-based approaches on other applications: computing generalized and fractional _hypertreewidth_, identifying the _perfect phylogeny_, or determining the _treelength_. As a last remark, another work proposed alternative practical techniques to compute the list of PMCs, using SAT and ASP declarative solvers \[23\].

## 1.2 Enumeration algorithms

Let us dive now into the details of PMC enumeration. Several results have been stated above, however the algorithm BT-enum \[6\] stands as the reference for enumerating PMCs in general graphs, even in practice \[21\]. We recall that its time complexity is \(\tilde{O}(|\Delta_G|^2)\), without any guarantee on the delay between two solution outputs (all PMCs might be returned to the very end of the execution of the algorithm). BT-enum uses simple but insightful observations on PMCs. It is a recursive algorithm: given a graph _G_, it begins with a recursive call on graph _G_\\{_a_} for some arbitrary vertex \(a\in V\) . Indeed, given the list of PMCs of _G_\\{_a_}, one can obtain all PMCs of _G_ following certain rules, recalled below.

On one hand, Bouchitté and Todinca \[6\] showed that the PMCs of _G_ containing _a_ can be written either \(S\cup\{a\}\) or \(\Omega'\cup\{a\}\), where _S_ is a minimal separator of _G_ and \(\Omega'\) is a PMC of _G_\\{_a_}. Since the enumeration of minimal separators is achieved in output-linear time \[1\] and that \(\Delta_G\le n|\Pi_G|\), checking whether all such sets are PMCs can be done in output-linear time after the recursive call. On the other hand, keeping identical notation, the PMCs which do not contain _a_ can be written either \(\Omega'\) or \(S\cup(C\cap T)\), where the additional variable _T_ is also a minimal separator of _G_ and _C_ is a connected component of _G_\\_S_ fully adjacent to _S_. The time complexity of BT-enum comes from this last costly case, where the check of all such sets \(S\cup(C\cap T)\) takes \(\tilde{O}(|\Delta_G|^2)=\tilde{O}(|\Pi_G|^2)\). BT-enum highlights the fact that PMCs can be enumerated in output-polynomial time, and more precisely in output-quadratic time. Handling differently the PMCs provided by this last costly case is the strategy we will adopt<tbc>

to decrease the running time for PMC enumeration.

Some alternative results on specific graph classes were proposed to decrease this output- quadratic running time. Several graph classes admit a number of PMCs which is polynomial in _n_: weakly chordal, polygon-circle, circular-arc, and _d_-trapezoid \[4, 14\]. BT-enum guarantees that, on graph classes with a number of PMCs (and hence minimal separators) polynomial in _n_, its running time is polynomial in _n_ too. Then, a very recent contribution was proposed in \[18\]: PMCs can be enumerated in polynomial delay on triconnected planar graphs, which gives thus an output-linear time on this large family of graphs. From a more parameterized viewpoint, two PMC enumeration algorithms were proposed \[13\] where the running time depends exponentially on respectively two parameters: _vertex cover_ and _modular width_.

BT-enum might use a quantity of memory exponential in _n_, since it is necessary to store all PMCs of _G_\\{_a_} but also all minimal separators of _G_ to return the final set \(\Pi_G\). It was shown very recently \[7\] that it is possible to modify BT-enum so that its running time stays output-polynomial while the memory used in the process is polynomial in _n_.

A natural technique in enumeration consists in looking at the _extension version_ of the enumeration problem: if this extension version can be solved in polynomial time, then it gives an enumeration algorithm with polynomial delay and space \[26\]. Such an approach - called _Flashlight Search_, but also sometimes _Backtrack_ or _Binary Partition_ - could be tried for PMC enumeration. The following problem is called PMC Extension: given a graph _G_, a _mandatory_ set \(M\subseteq V(G)\) and a _forbidden_ one \(F\subseteq V(G)\), is there a PMC \(\Omega\in\Pi_G\) satisfying \(M\subseteq\Omega\) and \(\Omega\cap F=\emptyset\)? Observe that PMC Extension is thus a decision problem. Being able to solve it in polynomial time would offer the possibility to "flashlight" PMCs, _i.e._ construct a binary decision tree, where each node represents a suitable partition (_M,F_) and each leaf is related to a unique PMC. Flashlight Search works for the enumeration of minimal separators in polynomial delay and space \[28\]. Unfortunately, we will show that such an approach will unlikely not work for PMC, strengthening our choice to propose different techniques.

## 1.3 Contributions and consequences

Our main contribution is the proposal of an output-linear time algorithm enumerating all PMCs of a graph.

**Theorem 1.** _Given a graph G with n_=|_V(G_)|_, one can compute the list of all PMCs of G in output-linear time_ \(\tilde{O}(|\Pi_G|)=O(n^4m|\Pi_G|)\).

Many literature results mentioned earlier looks like: given a graph _G_ with its lists of PMCs \(\Pi_G\), one can solve a problem P in time \(O(|\Pi_G|f_\mathcal{P}(n))\), where _f_<sub>P</sub> is some function depending on P. Thanks to Theorem 1, we can now get rid of this assumption that set \(\Pi_G\) is given. We can simply list the PMCs in output-linear time and then set \(\Pi_G\) is available, without affecting asymptotically the running time for problem P.

For example, as the time complexity of the enumeration of PMCs used to be in \(\tilde{O}(|\Delta_G|^2)\), we already had that the treewidth can be computed in \(\tilde{O}(|\Delta_G|^2)\), but this was potentially quadratic in the number of PMCs, since we have \(|\Pi_G|=\tilde{O}(|\Delta_G|)\) on certain graph classes. Our output-linear time enumeration of PMCs thus allows us to deduce an exact algorithm for treewidth whose running time depends linearly on the number of PMCs. The same observation<tbc>

holds for minimum fill-in, lis-(\(\text{tw}\le t\)) and max-(\(\text{tw}\le t,\varphi\)). Combining Theorem 1 with contributions in \[12, 14, 16\], we obtain the following corollary.

**Corollary 1.** _Given a graph G, an integer_ \(t\ge 0\) _and a CMS formula_ \(\varphi\)_, we have:_

• treewidth _and_ minimum fill-in _can be solved in_ \(\tilde{O}(|\Pi_G|)\),<tbc>

• lis-\((\text{\textit{tw}}\le t)\) _can be solved in_ \(O(n^{O(t)}|\Pi_G|)\),<tbc>

• max-\((\text{\textit{tw}}\le t,\varphi)\) _can be solved in_ \(O(n^{O(t)}\cdot f(t,\varphi)\cdot|\Pi_G|)\),

_without the need to possess initially the list of PMCs._

Let us describe briefly our approach for Theorem 1. Our algorithm, called PMC-Traversal, reuses some principles of BT-enum while developing a new technique which allows to decrease the overall running time. It is also recursive: it enumerates all PMCs by launching first a recursive call on a subgraph _G_\\{_a_} with an arbitrary vertex \(a\in V\) . The PMCs of _G_ containing _a_ - formed like \(S\cup\{a\}\) or \(\Omega'\cup\{a\}\) - are listed as in BT-enum. Also, as in BT-enum, all PMCs of _G_ which were PMCs of _G_\\{_a_} are enumerated easily thanks to the recursive call. The major difference between both algorithms lies in the way to enumerate PMCs of _G_ which are neither PMCs of _G_\\{_a_} nor containing _a_. Instead of listing brute-forcely all pairs of minimal separators of _G_, we introduce a novel and completely different technique to achieve this task: we execute a traversal of some "PMC-graph", whose nodes are PMCs and edges define a notion of neighborhood between PMCs. This approach was inspired by the _Proximity Search_ framework \[10\].

More concretely, we define a neighborhood relation \(\mathcal{N}\in\Pi_G\times\Pi_G\) which associates any PMC with a collection of neighbors. Relation N is fast to handle, since any PMC admits at most _n_<sup>2</sup> neighbors and, moreover, these neighbors can be computed in time polynomial in _n_. The PMC-graph mentioned above is then the graph \((\Pi_G,\mathcal{N})\). Naturally, this graph is partially known even after exploiting the recursive call, since otherwise all PMCs would have already been listed. Our idea consists of traversing the PMC-graph, starting from the PMCs already enumerated (PMCs containing _a_ or PMCs of _G_\\{_a_}), exploring their neighbors through N and so on. Said differently, we launch a _Breadth-First Search_ (BFS) whose initial queue contains the PMCs already enumerated, and the edges visited are given by relation N. We show that this procedure allows us to attain any PMC of _G_.

By the way, a large part of the paper is dedicated to the proof of this latter statement. An essential tool to complete this proof consists, at some moment, in deciding whether some given set _X_ contains (or not) a PMC \(\Omega\subseteq X\), and, if yes, producing such \(\Omega\). We call this problem PMC Superset. Observe that PMC Superset is a special case of PMC Extension defined above, fixing \(M=\emptyset\). We show that PMC Superset is polynomial-time solvable.

**Theorem 2.** _There is an algorithm deciding_ PMC Superset _in time O(n_<sup>3</sup>_m). Furthermore, for a yes-instance, it produces a solution PMC._

One may wonder what is the computational complexity of the more general PMC Extension problem, since a polynomial-time algorithm for it would imply polynomial delay for PMC enumeration, which is stronger than Theorem 1. We provide a NP-hardness proof, using a 3-SAT reduction. This proof is preceded by another NP-hardness reduction for Minimal (_a,b_)-separator Extension which stands as an intermediary step.

**Theorem 3.** PMC Extension _is NP-complete._

### 1.4 Perspectives

Even if our algorithm produces PMCs in output-linear time, it provides no guarantee on the delay between two outputs. In fact, we are even sure that the time taken before the return of the first PMC of _G_ cannot be less than exponential in _n_, because of the recursive nature of our procedure (as for BT-enum). Hence, finding a polynomial-delay enumeration algorithm for PMCs remains an open challenge. We wonder whether the traversal of the PMC-graph - our approach introduced to improve BT-enum - could not be itself a polynomial-delay algorithm enumerating PMCs. Concretely, one could compute one arbitrary PMC of _G_, fix it as a single element in the starting queue of a BFS, and explore the PMC-graph using our neighborhood relation N. For sure, the running time between two solutions would be polynomial in _n_ as all neighbors of a PMC can be determined fast. However, the main question is whether all PMCs would be enumerated with this method. We did not identify promising directions to prove this statement so far. But this BFS did not miss any PMCs on the numerous graph classes we tested experimentally, although we are blocked computationally by the brute-force checking (at most 20 vertices).

Another natural question is whether output-linear time can be maintained while only polynomial space is used. To reach this goal, one could think of exploring the recursion tree in a DFS manner, as done in \[7\]. Perhaps such an approach stands also as another promising direction to obtain polynomial-time delay.

Fomin and Villanger \[15\] showed that, for any integer \(k\ge 1\), knowing the list \(\Pi_G^{k+1}\) of PMCs of size at most _k_+1 allows checking whether the input graph _G_ has treewidth at most _k_ in time linear in \(|\Pi_G^{k+1}|\).<sup>3</sup> As a direct consequence, the existence of an FPT-output-linear time algorithm enumerating PMCs of small size would be a significant result, _i.e._ with running time \(O(f(k)n^{O(1)}|\Pi_G^k|)\) where _f_ is an arbitrary function and \(\Pi_G^k\) is the set of PMCs of size at most _k_. Indeed, it would give an algorithm deciding whether treewidth is at most _k_ in time \(\tilde{O}(f(k)|\Pi_G^k|)\), which could be very efficient in practice.

A final perspective is simply to implement our algorithm. The experimental study produced in \[21\], which displays numerous benchmarks of algorithms/instances, could be extended with our improvement for PMC enumeration. Such an experimental contribution would allow assessing in practice the performance gain offered by output-linear time, instead of output-quadratic one.

## 2 Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce some general notation and concepts related to connectivity in graphs. We also define the notion of _Potential Maximal Clique_ (PMC) and provide some observations.

### 2.1 General graph notations

All graphs mentioned in this paper are simple, finite, undirected, unweighted and connected. Any graph _G_=(_V,E_) is given with _V_ a set of _n_ vertices and \(E\subseteq V\times V\) a set of _m_ edges. As we will sometimes handle several graphs in parallel, function \(V(\cdot)\) will provide the vertex set of a graph, and \(E(\cdot)\) its edge set: here, _V(G_)=_V_ and _E(G_)=_E_. Given a set of<tbc>

<sup>3</sup>Separators of size at most _k_ are also needed.

<tbc>vertices \(U\subseteq V\) , the notation <o>_U_</o> refers to the complementary of _U_ in _V_ : <o>_U_</o>=_V_\\_U_. We say two vertices _u_ and _v_ are adjacent in _G_ if \((u,v)\in E\). For any vertex \(u\in V\) , we denote respectively by \(N(u)=\{v:(u,v)\in E\}\) the _open neighborhood_<sup>4</sup> of _u_ and \(N[u]=N(u)\cup\{u\}\) its _close neighborhood_. These notions are naturally generalized to sets: for any \(U\subseteq V\) , \(N(U)=\{v:(u,v)\in E,u\in U,v\notin U\}\) and \(N[U]=U\cup N(U)\).

A _path P_ from _a_ to _b_ of _G_ is a sequence of vertices (_v_<sub>0</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>2</sub>_,...,v_<sub>_k_-1</sub>_,v<sub>k</sub>_) such that _a=v_<sub>0</sub>_,b=v<sub>k</sub>_, and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for any \(0\le i<k\). Concisely, we say that _P_ is an (_a,b_)-path. A _simple path_ is a path without any repetition of vertices. From now on, the term _path_ will automatically refer to the notion of simple path. A graph _G_ is _connected_ if for any pair of vertices \(a,b\in V\) , \(a\neq b\), there is an (_a,b_)-path in _G_.

A _subgraph_ \(G'\) of _G_ is a graph \(G'=(V',E')\) made up of a subset of vertices/edges of _G_, formally \(V'\subseteq V\) and \(E'\subseteq E\cap(V'\times V')\). For any \(V'\subseteq V\) , we denote \(G[V']=(V',E\cap(V'\times V'))\) the _induced subgraph_ of \(V'\). Its edge set will be written briefly as \(E[V']=E\cap(V'\times V')\). Given a vertex set \(U\subseteq V\) , let _G_\\_U_ denote the graph _G_ deprived of vertices in _U_, formally _G_\\_U=G_\[<o>_U_</o>\]. More generally, given two sets _A_ and _B_ such that \(A\subseteq B\), then _B_\\_A_ denote the set _B_ deprived of elements of _A_.

Finally, we distinguish between the notion of _subset_ which includes equality (symbol \(\subseteq\)) and _proper subset_ which refers necessarily to a smaller set (symbol \(\unknown\)).

## 2.2 Connectivity and separators

### 2.2.1 Connectivity

We introduce now standard notations of connectivity, beginning with connected components.

**Definition 1** (Connected components)**.** _Consider a graph G. Let U be a set of vertices_ \(U\unknown V(G)\) _and let_ \(a\notin U\)_. We denote respectively by:_

• _C<sub>G</sub>(a,U_) _the_ connected component _of G_\\_U which contains a,_<tbc>

• _C<sub>G</sub>_\[_a,U_\] _the corresponding_ close connected component:

\(C_G[a,U]=C_G(a,U)\cup(U\cap N_G(C_G(a,U))).\)

_When G is clear from the context, we will sometimes remove it from subscript and use simply C(a,U_) _and C_\[_a,U_\].

We pursue with the concept of _full component_, which is a common notion related to both minimal separators and PMCs. A full component is simply a connected component which admits the whole removed set in its neighborhood.

**Definition 2** (Full components \[6\])**.** _Consider a graph G and a vertex set_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\)_. We say a connected component C of G_\\_U is a_ full component _for U if the neighborhood of the component in G is exactly U, formally N(C_)=_U._

Said differently, if some connected component _C<sub>G</sub>(a,U_) is a full component for _U_, then \(C_G[a,U]=C_G(a,U)\cup U\). We will see in the remainder that a minimal separator _S_ admits full components, but this is not the case for a PMC.

<sup>4</sup>We will use notation _N<sub>G</sub>(u_) when _G_ is not absolutely clear from the context.

**Definition 3** (Shy set)**.** _Consider a graph G and a vertex set_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\)_. We say that U is a_ shy set _if there is no connected component of G_\\_U which is a full component for U. Formally, for any connected component C of G_\\_U,_ \(N_G(C)\neq U\).

Observe that if some set _U_ is shy, then naturally any of its superset is also shy, otherwise a full component for the superset would imply necessarily a full component for _U_ in _G_\\_U_. Trivially, _V(G_) is always a shy set.

**Observation 1.** _Given a shy set_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\) _of G, any of its superset_ \(W\supseteq U\) _is also shy._

Another common notion widely used in the context of treewidth is the _torso_.

**Definition 4** (Torso \[25, 27\])**.** _Consider a graph G and some set_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\)_. The graph torso(G,U_) _has vertex set U and its edge set is made up of all edges_ \((u,v)\in U\times U\) _satisfying either_ \((u,v)\in E(G)\) _or there is a_ (_u,v)-path of G whose internal vertices are not in U._

Torsos characterize, given a vertex set _U_, its connectivity outside _U_, _i.e._ either through direct edges between two vertices or through paths outside _U_. For tree decompositions, torsos are used to characterize the connectivity between vertices of the same bag. In this paper, the torso will be a tool manipulated to not only define PMCs but also to introduce their properties.

We extend the notion of neighborhood into a larger (natural) one that we call _reachability_. Again, if we consider some vertex set \(U\subseteq V(G)\), reachability defines, given some vertex \(u\in U\), the set of vertices which can be reached from _u_ using only intermediary vertices outside _U_.

**Definition 5** (Reachability)**.** _Let U be a set of vertices_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\) _and a vertex_ \(u\in U\)_. We define as R<sub>G</sub>(u,U_) _the set of vertices of U which can be reached from u either directly (with an edge) or via intermediary vertices which are outside U._

_Two equivalent and more formal definitions follow._ \(v\in R_G(u,U)\) _if and only if:_

• _either_ \((u,v)\in E(G)\) _or there is a path in G starting from u and arriving at v such that all its internal vertices belong to <o>U</o>=V(G_)\\_U._<tbc>

• \((u,v)\in E(\mathtt{torso}(G,U))\).

Note that in this definition, set _R<sub>G</sub>(u,U_) is a subset of _U_ and can be seen as the neighborhood of _u_ in torso(_G,U_). Nevertheless, we will sometimes need a broader notion of reachability which contains the vertices outside _U_ also.

**Definition 6** (Global reachability)**.** _Let U be a set of vertices_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\) _and some vertex_ \(a\in V(G)\)_. We fix_ \(R_G^+(a,U)\) _the set of vertices of G which can be reached from a either via some direct edge or through some path whose internal vertices belong to <o>U</o>._

Note that there are two changes compared to Definition 5: first vertex _a_ is not necessarily in _U_, second set \(R_G^+(a,U)\) is not a subset of _U_: it also contains vertices of <o>_U_</o> reachable from _a_ via paths outside _U_. In the case \(u\in U\), then \(R_G(u,U)=R_G^+(u,U)\cap U\). All these aspects are illustrated in Figure 1. We can now introduce some vocabulary related to reachability.

**Definition 7** (Reachability property and conflicts)**.** _Let_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\) _be a set of vertices and_ \(u,v\in U\)_. We say that:_

• _Vertices u and v are_ visible despite _U if_ \(v\in R_G(u,U)\) _- equivalently_ \(u\in R_G(v,U)\) _as G is undirected. Another formulation we will use for this statement is either (i) u sees v despite U or (ii) u and v_ see each other _despite U._<tbc>

• _Conversely, vertices u and v are_ in conflict _for U if_ \(v\notin R_G(u,U)\)_. Another possible formulation used is that_ (_u,v_) _is a_ conflict pair _for U._<tbc>

• _Vertex u is_ enlightened _for U if it is not involved in any conflict pair: R<sub>G</sub>(u,U_)=_U._<tbc>

• _Set U satisfies the_ reachability property _if, for any pair_ \(x,y\in U\)_, x and y are visible despite U._

Naturally, by considering a subset \(U'\subseteq U\) where _U_ has the reachability property, we preserve the property as the graph \(G\backslash U'\) is less restricted than _G_\\_U_ in terms of connectivity. More concretely, two reachable vertices \(x,y\in U'\) in _G_\\_U_ are still reachable in \(G\backslash U'\). Trivially, the empty set and singletons always have the reachability property.

**Observation 2.** _Given a set U that satisfies the reachability property, any subset of U also satisfies it._

## 2.3 A story of potential maximal cliques

Initially, PMCs were defined as a key tool for designing a divide-and-conquer algorithm computing the treewidth of an input graph \[3\]. Their original definition comes with the notion of _triangulation_. A graph _G_ is _chordal_ if every cycle of length at least 4 has a chord. A<tbc>

<tbc>triangulation represents a way to add edges to some graph _G_ in order to make it chordal. Treewidth and triangulations are very close concepts: computing the treewidth of a graph amounts to finding a triangulation with the smallest clique size.

**Definition 13** (Triangulation \[20\])**.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be any graph. We say that a graph H is a_ triangulation _of G if both H is chordal and is obtained by adding edges to G,_ i.e. \(H=(V,E\cup F)\)_, where_ \(E\cap F=\emptyset\).

_A_ minimal triangulation _H of G is a triangulation of G for which H_\\{_e_} _is not chordal, for any_ \(e\in F\).

PMCs are exactly the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of _G_.

**Definition 14** (Potential Maximal Clique (PMC))**.** _A set_ \(\Omega\subseteq V(G)\) _is a_ potential maximal clique _(PMC) of G if_ \(\Omega\) _is an inclusion-wise maximal clique of some minimal triangulation of G._

**Theorem 4** (\[6\])**.** _Let G be a graph and_ \(\Omega\subseteq V(G)\)_. Set_ \(\Omega\) _is a PMC iff it satisfies the two following properties:_

• \(\Omega\) _is a shy set._<tbc>

• \(\Omega\) _has the reachability property._

From now on, this latter characterization will be the main method used to identify PMCs. Thanks to it, we can check whether some set is a PMC or not in polynomial time.

**Lemma 7** (PMC identification \[6\])**.** _Given a set_ \(\Omega\subseteq V(G)\)_, we can decide in O(nm_) _whether_ \(\Omega\) _is a PMC of G or not._

In the literature, many properties of PMCs were identified. Most of them concern the case where _G_ is not a complete graph. Indeed, if _G_ is a clique, then it admits a unique PMC _V(G_), as any other vertex set is not shy. For this reason, we focus in this paper only on graphs _G_ which are not complete, to skip this trivial but specific case. On other graphs, PMCs and minimal separators admit strong connections.

A first property of PMCs is that none of their proper subset is a PMC.

**Lemma 8** (\[6\])**.** _Any_ \(PMC\Omega'\) _of G cannot be strictly included into another_ \(PMC\Omega\) _of G._

This comes from the fact that, as PMCs have the reachability property, any proper subset admits at least one full component - the one which contains a removed vertex. Observe that this statement also holds for minimal (_a,b_)-separators with fixed (_a,b_), but not for minimal separators in a broad sense.

Second, an interesting fact is that the neighborhood of any connected component of \(G\backslash\Omega\), for any \(PMC\Omega\), is a minimal separator of _G_.

**Lemma 9** (\[6\])**.** _For any_ \(PMC\Omega\) _of G, the minimal separators of G which are included into_ \(\Omega\) _are exactly the sets N<sub>G</sub>(C), for any connected component C of_ \(G\backslash\Omega\)_. Those sets are called_ neighbor separators.

Many efforts in the study of PMCs are dedicated to the structural features of these neighbor separators \(S\subseteq\Omega\). We pursue with a property of sets \(\Omega\backslash S\), which are PMCs without one of its neighbor separator.

**Lemma 10** (\[6\])**.** _Let_ \(\Omega\) _be a PMC of G and S a minimal separator of G contained in_ \(\Omega\)_. The set_ \(\Omega\backslash S\) _is included into one connected component of G_\\_S which is full for S._

One aspect of neighbor separators is crucial to achieve the analysis of both BT-Enum \[6\] and our algorithm PMC-Traversal. It concerns the impact of _triangulating_ these separators \(S\unknown\Omega\), _i.e._ adding all possible edges in \(S\times S\).

**Definition 15** (Active separator \[6\])**.** _Let_ \(\Omega\) _be a PMC of G and_ \(S\subseteq\Omega\) _a minimal separator of G. We say S is active for_ \(\Omega\) _if_ \(\Omega\) _is not a clique after triangulating all neighbor separators_ \(S'\unknown\Omega\) _different from S, i.e._ \(S'\neq S\)_. PMCs which admit at least one active separator are called_ active PMCs.

A surprising point is that the notion of active separator is in some way related to the property of being (or not) a PMC in subgraphs of _G_. We define _a-nice PMCs_, reusing an expression from \[15\].

**Definition 16** (_a_-nice PMC)**.** _Given a graph G and some vertex_ \(a\in V(G)\)_, we say a PMC_ \(\Omega\) _of G is a_-nice _iff_ \(a\notin\Omega\) _and_ \(\Omega\) _is not a PMC of graph G_\\{_a}._

Authors of \[6\] established that if \(\Omega\) is a PMC of _G_ but not of _G_\\{_a_}, then necessarily the singleton {_a_} in _G_ is a one-vertex separator which blocks the reachability between at least two vertices of \(\Omega\). Consequently, the separator \(S=N(C_G(a,\Omega))\) is active: as {_a_} is sufficient to separate some pair \(u,v\in\Omega\) in \(G[\overline{\Omega}\cup\{u,v\}]\), then for any connected component _C_ of \(G\backslash\Omega\) different from \(C_G(a,\Omega)\), we cannot have \(\{u,v\}\subseteq N(C)\). So, triangulating all separators _N(C_) with \(C\neq C_G(a,\Omega)\) will not make \(\Omega\) become a clique, since edge (_u,v_) will miss. This is why _a_-nice PMCs are also active PMCs. The base case of the recursion is the enumeration of PMCs in the single-vertex graph, which is trivial. The output-quadratic running time of BT-enum comes from the fourth case, which consists in enumerating all pairs of minimal separators of _G_. The first three cases cost a time linear in the number of PMCs, in particular the third one which uses the polynomial-delay enumeration of minimal separators (Lemma 1) and exploits the inequality \(|\Delta_G|\le n|\Pi_G|\). Such shy decomposition can be obtained by picking any minimal separator of \(\Omega\) and then applying the procedure of Lemma 15 until obtaining an \(\Omega\)-shy separator _S_ with regard to the component containing \(\Omega\backslash S\).

**Definition 19** (Shy decomposition)**.** _Given a graph G and one of its PMCs_ \(\Omega\)_, a pair_ (_S,T_) _is a_ shy decomposition _of_ \(\Omega\) _if it satisfies the following properties:_

• (_S,T_) _is a partition of_ \(\Omega\): \(S\cup T=\Omega\) _and_ \(S\cap T=\emptyset\),<tbc>

• _S is a minimal separator of G which is_ \(\Omega\)_-shy with regard to C, where C=C<sub>G</sub>(t,S_) _with_ \(t\in T\).

Lemma 15 guarantees that each PMC admits at least one shy decomposition. Before going further on PMC Superset, we state an important connection between the concepts of shy separators and active separators. The following result is used in Section 4.

**Lemma 16.** _Consider a graph G with a PMC_ \(\Omega\) _which admits an active separator S. Let C be the connected component of G_\\_S containing_ \(T=\Omega\backslash S\)_. Then, separator S is_ \(\Omega\)_-shy with regard to C._

_Proof._ Assume by way of contradiction that _S_ is not \(\Omega\)-shy with regard to _C_. There exists a connected component \(B\unknown C\) in \(G\backslash\Omega\) which is full for _S_: \(S\subseteq N(B)\). Hence, for any pair \(x,y\in S\), set _T_ does not separate pair (_x,y_) in graph \(G[C\cup\{x,y\}]\): indeed, there is a (_x,y_)-path whose internal vertices belong to _B_, as both \(x,y\in N(B)\). This contradicts the fact that _S_ is active (Definition 15).

## 3.3 A characterization of PMC supersets

The presence of a shy separator is the key witness to assess whether some shy set is a PMC superset. We begin with "if" part: if some set _X_ is a PMC superset, then there is necessarily a shy separator \(S\unknown X\). The formal statement is provided below.

**Theorem 6.** _Let_ \(X\subseteq V(G)\) _be a shy set. If X is a PMC superset, then there exists a triplet_ (_a,b,S_) _satisfying the following properties:_

• _a and b are two distinct vertices and in particular_ \(a\in X\),<tbc>

• _S is the X-close_ (_a,b)-separator,_<tbc>

• _S is an X-shy separator with regard to C<sub>G</sub>(a,S)._<tbc>

_Proof._ As _X_ is a PMC superset, there exists a PMC \(\Omega\subseteq X\). According to Lemma 15, \(\Omega\) admits a shy decomposition \((S',T')\), where separator \(S'\) is \(\Omega\)-shy with regards to \(C'\), which is the connected component in \(G\backslash S'\) containing \(T'\). We fix arbitrarily \(a\in T\subseteq C'\) and _b_ as a vertex belonging to any other full component for \(S'\) in _G_. By definition of both of these vertices, \(S'\) is a minimal (_a,b_)-separator, and \(S'\unknown X\). See Figure 8 for an illustration.

Let _S_ be the _X_-close (_a,b_)-separator. Since \(S'\unknown X\), from Lemma 6, _S_ and \(S'\) are parallel and \(C_G(a,S)\subseteq C_G(a,S')=C'\). We fix _C=C<sub>G</sub>(a,S_). Assume by way of contradiction that _S_ is not _X_-shy with regards to _C_. Then, there exists a connected component _B_ of _G_\[_C_\[_X_\] which is fully adjacent to _S_. As \(B\subseteq C\backslash X\), we also have \(B\subseteq C'\backslash\Omega\) because \(C\backslash X\subseteq C'\backslash X\subseteq C'\backslash\Omega\), using the inclusion properties stated so far. Let us call \(B'\) the connected component of \(G[C'\backslash\Omega]\) containing _B_. We show that \(S'\subseteq N_G(B')\).

Let \(s\in S'\). If \(s\in S'\cap S\), then _s_ is adjacent to \(B\subseteq B'\) because _B_ is full for _S_. Otherwise, assume \(s\in S'\backslash S\). Since \(\Omega\) is a PMC of _G_ and has the reachability property, there exists an (_a,s_)-path _P<sub>s</sub>_ whose internal vertices belong to \(\overline{\Omega}\) (if there are). As _S_ is closer to _a_ than \(S'\), _i.e._ \(C_G(a,S)\subseteq C_G(a,S')\), path _P<sub>s</sub>_ intersects _S_. Said differently, _P<sub>s</sub>_ contains a vertex \(v\in S\cap\overline{\Omega}\). Since _B_ is fully adjacent to _S_ and \(v\notin\Omega\), we have \(v\in B'\). Due to the presence of the internal vertex \(v\in B'\) in path _P<sub>s</sub>_ - which has internal vertices in \(\overline{\Omega}\) - then all internal vertices of _P<sub>s</sub>_ belong to \(B'\) and thus _s_ is adjacent to \(B'\).

In summary, \(B'\) is a connected component of \(G[C'\backslash\Omega]\) full for \(S'\): a contradiction since we assumed that \(S'\) is \(\Omega\)-shy with regard to \(C'\). Consequently, _S_ is _X_-shy with regard to _C_, completing the proof.

### 3.4 A polynomial-time algorithm for PMC superset

The characterization of PMC supersets established in Corollary 2 provides us with a way to check whether some shy set _X_ is a PMC superset. Indeed, it suffices to determine the existence (or not) of a triplet (_a,b,S_) satisfying the properties listed in Corollary 2. It becomes rapidly clear that answering the latter question can be achieved in time polynomial in _n_. One can simply enumerate all possible pairs \(a,b\in V(G)\) and then compute the unique _X_-close (_a,b_)-separator _S_. The last check consists in looking at the shyness of _S_, which is a simple connectivity property. All in all, we obtain a polynomial-time complexity for PMC Superset.

**Theorem 2.** _There is an algorithm deciding_ PMC Superset _in time O(n_<sup>3</sup>_m). Furthermore, for a yes-instance, it produces a solution PMC._

_Proof._ We begin with the research of a triplet (_a,b,S_). First, we enumerate all pairs of vertices \((a,b)\in X\times V(G)\) and check whether \((a,b)\notin E(G)\) and _X_\\{_a_} is an (_a,b_)-separator. If these conditions are not satisfied, we move on to another pair. Otherwise, we compute the _X_-close (_a,b_)-separator _S_. By Definition 12, constructing the _X_-close (_a,b_)-separator consists first in determining set _A=C<sub>G</sub>(a,X_\\{_a_}): it can be achieved with a BFS starting at _a_ in graph _G_\\(_X_\\{_a_}). Second, we compute _S_=S_<sub>G</sub>(A,b_) in linear time (Lemma 4). When _S_ is known, we check whether it is _X_-shy with regard to _C=C<sub>G</sub>(a,S_). Concretely, we compute graph _G_\[_C_\\_X_\] with its connected components: for each of them, we look at their neighborhood and verify whether _S_ is included into it. This takes _O(nm_). In summary, checking the presence of a triplet (_a,b,S_) witnessing the presence of PMC inside _X_ can be achieved by enumerating all pairs (_a,b_) and then verifying whether the _X_-close (_a,b_)-separator exists and is _X_-shy. The running time is _O(n_<sup>3</sup>_m_).

If no triplet satisfies the conditions listed in Corollary 2, then we conclude that _X_ is not a PMC superset. But if one works, then we can compute a PMC \(\Omega\subseteq X\) in _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) (Corollary 2) and we answer that _X_ is indeed a PMC superset. The overall running time to decide PMC superset is thus _O(n_<sup>3</sup>_m_).

This section is dedicated to the description and the analysis of our algorithm PMC-Traversal which enumerates all PMCs of a graph in output-linear time. The previous section will be used as a toolkit to attain this objective.

## 4.1 Presentation of the algorithm: an extension of Bouchitté-Todinca method

Our algorithm PMC-Traversal can be seen as an extension of BT-Enum. We will keep its outline while improving the bottleneck step. Indeed, the fourth step of BT-Enum determines completely its worst-case time complexity. For the three first steps, we still do the same as BT-Enum, since these steps already cost output-linear time. The base case (_G_ is a clique, line 4 of Algorithm 3) takes _O_(1) time and satisfies the previous inequality (if no, then _K_ could adjusted to a larger value but still constant). ## 5 Hardness results

We provide in this section polynomial reductions from 3-SAT to two extension problems: Minimal (_a,b_)-separator Extension and PMC Extension. Finally, we show that in, our reduced instance for PMC Extension,the constraint on forbidden vertices can be withdrawn. This allows us to conclude the NP-hardness of PMC Subset, which is PMC Extension with the restriction \(F=\emptyset\).

Our proof that PMC Extension is NP-hard is strongly related to the construction of \(G(\Phi)\) in the previous subsection. We proceed by showing that identifying a PMC extending _M_ in \(G(\Phi)\) is equivalent to finding a minimal (_a,b_)-separator extending _M_ in \(G(\Phi)\). First, we establish some properties of PMCs in graph \(G(\Phi)\).

**Lemma 20.** _In graph_ \(G(\Phi)\)_, we have_ \(N[a]\cup N[b]=V(G(\Phi))\)_. For any_ \(MC\Omega\) _of_ \(G(\Phi)\) _such that_ \(\Omega\cap\{a,b\}=\emptyset\)_, there are exactly two connected components in_ \(G\backslash\Omega\)_, which are_ \(C(a,\Omega)\) _and_ \(C(b,\Omega)\).

_Proof._ From graph construction, \(N[a]\cup N[b]=V(G(\Phi))\) and \(N[a]\cap N[b]=\emptyset\). Assume that _a_ and _b_ belong to the same connected component _C_ of \(G\backslash\Omega\), then _C_ is necessarily a full component for \(\Omega\) since \(\Omega\subseteq N(a)\cup N(b)\), contradicting Theorem 4. So, \(G\backslash\Omega\) admits at least two connected components, containing respectively _a_ and _b_. There cannot be a third one \(C'\), since \(C'\subseteq N(a)\cup N(b)\).

**Lemma 21.** _For any_ (_a,b)-separator S of_ \(G(\Phi)\) _extending M and any vertex_ \(x\in C(a,S)\) _(resp._ \(\in C(b,S)\)_), there is_ \(v\in S\) _such that_ \(N(v)\cap C(a,S)=\{x\}\) _(resp._ \(N(v)\cap C(b,S)=\{x\}\)_)._

_Proof._ Any (_a,b_)-separator _S_ of \(G(\Phi)\) is a superset of some minimal (_a,b_)-separator of \(G(\Phi)\), which is, from the claim of Theorem 12, some \(S(\sigma)\). Hence, for some truth assignment \(\sigma\), \(S(\sigma)\subseteq S\). Consider any \(x\in C(a,S)\): it can thus be either _a_ or some vertex in \(\{\alpha_i,\overline{\alpha_i}\}_{1\le i\le n}\). If _x=a_, then pick _v_ as any vertex \(\alpha_i\) or \(\overline{\alpha_i}\) belonging to _S_. The neighborhood of _v_ in _C(a,S_) contains only _a_. Else, if \(x=\alpha_i\) w.l.o.g. (case \(x=\overline{\alpha_i}\) works similarly by symmetry), then it means that \(\overline{\beta_i}\) belongs necessarily to _S_, hence with \(v=\overline{\beta_i}\), we have \(N(v)\cap C(a,S)=\{\alpha_i\}\). We can achieve the same reasoning on side _C(b,S_), the only difference being the adjacency between vertices in \(\{\beta_i,\overline{\beta_i}\}_{1\le i\le n}\) with clause vertices, but since the latter belongs to \(M\unknown S\), it has no impact.

We pursue with a key lemma which presents the form of PMCs in \(G(\Phi)\) which both extends _M_ and do not contain _a_ and _b_. In fact, they are very close to the separators \(S(\sigma)\) introduced in Theorem 12. In the remainder, for any \(1\le j\le m\), we denote by _B(C<sub>j</sub>_) the set of \(\beta\)-vertices adjacent to the clause vertex _C<sub>j</sub>_, formally \(B(C_j)=N(C_j)\cap\{\beta_i,\overline{\beta_i}\}_{1\le i\le n}\).

**Lemma 22.** _If_ \(\Omega\) _is a PMC of_ \(G(\Phi)\) _extending M and such that_ \(a,b\notin\Omega\)_, then the following statements hold:_

• _there is exactly one index_ \(1\le i\le n\) _such that_ |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=3 _with_ \(T_i=\{\alpha_i,\overline{\alpha_i},\beta_i,\overline{\beta_i}\}\cap\Omega\);<tbc>

• _for all other indices_ \(1\le p\neq i\le n\)_, we have_ |_T<sub>p</sub>_|=2 _with_ \(T_p=\{\alpha_p,\beta_p\}\) _or_ \(T_p=\{\overline{\alpha_p},\overline{\beta_p}\}\).<tbc>

• _for any_ \(1\le j\le m\), \(B(C_j)\backslash\Omega\neq\emptyset\).

_Proof._ We proceed by case disjunction. From Lemma 20, vertices _a_ and _b_ cannot belong to the same connected component. For any \(1\le i\le n\), if |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=0 or 1, there would be an (_a,b_)- path in \(G\backslash\Omega\), which is impossible. Case |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=4 cannot occur either because there would be neither a direct edge nor a path with internal vertices in \(\overline{\Omega}\) between \(\alpha_i\) and \(\beta_i\). Indeed, we are blocked not only by vertices in _T<sub>i</sub>_ but also by clause vertices.

In the following, we show that we cannot have |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=2 for all \(1\le i\le n\). First, we exclude the case where \(\Omega\) contains, for some index _i_, pairs \(\alpha_i\overline{\beta_i}\) or \(\overline{\alpha_i}\beta_i\) because it leads to a path from _a_ to _b_ in \(G\backslash\Omega\) (Lemma 20). Then, there is only three configurations for each _i_ to consider :<tbc>

(1) \(T_i=\alpha_i\overline{\alpha_i}\),<tbc>

(2) \(T_i=\beta_i\overline{\beta_i}\)<tbc>

(3) \(T_i=\alpha_i\beta_i\) or \(\overline{\alpha_i\beta_i}\)

If all _x<sub>i</sub>_ are in the case (1), then we have \(C(b,\Omega)\) has a full component for \(\Omega\). Same for the case (2) and \(C(a,\Omega)\). If all _x<sub>i</sub>_ are in case (3), then \(C(a,\Omega)\) is a full component for \(\Omega\). If we mix only the cases (1) and (2), then we have the _b<sub>i</sub>_ of an index _i_ in case (1) that cannot see an \(a_{i^\prime}\) of an index \(i'\) in case (2) despite \(\Omega\). If we blend the case (1) and the case (3), then we have either no full component if there is a _C<sub>j</sub>_ such that \(B(C_j)\backslash\Omega=\emptyset\) but vertex _C<sub>j</sub>_ will not reach any \(b_{i^\prime}\) in the case (1). If we mix case (2) and the case (3), then _C(a,S_) is a full component for \(\Omega\).

In brief, we cannot have |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=2 for all indices \(1\le i\le n\). We finally show that we cannot have more than one _x<sub>i</sub>_ with |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=3. With |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=3, there is a vertex \(u\in T_i\) not adjacent to \(C(a,\Omega)\) and another vertex _v_ not adjacent to \(C(b,\Omega)\). For any pair of \(x_i,x_{i^\prime}\) such that \(|T_i|=|T_{i^\prime}|=3\), the vertex _u_ (resp. _v_) of _T<sub>i</sub>_ cannot reach the vertex \(v'\) (resp \(u'\)) of \(T_{i^\prime}\).

At last, if there is exactly one _x<sub>i</sub>_ with |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=3, then all other _x<sub>p</sub>_, with \(p\neq i\) have |_T<sub>p</sub>_|=2. Furthermore, variable gadgets with |_T<sub>p</sub>_|=2 cannot be in the case (1) or (2) because they would create a conflict pair with the gadget _T<sub>i</sub>_. Indeed, _T<sub>i</sub>_ contains exactly one vertex not adjacent to \(C(a,\Omega)\) and one vertex not adjacent to \(C(b,\Omega)\). Another gadget _T<sub>p</sub>_ in case (1) or (2) contains either a vertex not adjacent to \(C(a,\Omega)\) or a vertex not adjacent to \(C(b,\Omega)\). As a conclusion, all |_T<sub>p</sub>_|=2 are in the case (3). Furthermore, we have also that \(\forall j,B(C_j)\backslash\Omega\neq\emptyset\) because otherwise, gadgets in case (3) would only admit \(C(a,\Omega)\) as a full component. It follows that the vertex of the gadget with |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=3 which is disconnected to \(C(a,\Omega)\) would not reach one clause vertex with covered \(\beta\)-vertices.

These different elements on the structures of PMCs extending _M_ and avoiding _a,b_ reveal the form already found in Theorem 12: these PMCs seem strongly related to the truth assignment of the SAT formula \(\Phi\). We confirm this intuition, showing that PMC Extension and Minimal (_a,b_)-separator Extension are equivalent problems on this setting.

**Lemma 23.** _In_ \(G(\Phi)\)_, there exists a PMC_ \(\Omega\) _extending M and such that_ \(a,b\notin\Omega\) _iff there exist a minimal_ (_a,b)-separator S extending M._

_Proof._ **Only if direction.** Given a minimal (_a,b_)-separator _S_ of \(G(\Phi)\) extending _M_, \(G(\Phi)\backslash S\) admits two full components _C(a,S_) and _C(b,S_). We can add an extra vertex _x_ of any variable gadget into _S_: we say w.l.o.g. that \(x\in C(a,S)\). By Lemma 21, there exists \(v\in S\) such that \(N(v)\cap C(a,S)=\{x\}\), so for set \(X=S\cup\{a\}\), _C(a,X_) is not a full component for _X_. Moreover, _C(b,X_) is not a full component either for _X_, since \(x\in C(a,S)\). Set _X_ is shy. Moreover, as _C(a,S_) was a full component for _S_, vertex _x_ is enlightened for _X_. As _C(b,S_) was also a full component for _S_, vertices of _S_ see each other via this connected component. Consequently, _X_ has the reachability property and is a PMC.

**If direction.** Given a PMC \(\Omega\) satisfying \(M\unknown\Omega\) and \(\Omega\cap\{a,b\}=\emptyset\), we know by Lemma 22 that we have two vertices picked up in every gadgets except for one where there are three. By Lemma 20, we know that \(G(\Phi)\backslash\Omega\) has exactly two connected components: \(C(a,\Omega)\) and \(C(b,\Omega)\). Now consider the variable gadget with |_T<sub>i</sub>_|=3. We distinguish two cases:

• _T<sub>i</sub>_ contains all \(\beta\)-vertices: in this setting, the separator \(S=N(C(a,\Omega))\) contains every vertex of _M_. It follows, by Lemma 9, that _S_ is a minimal (_a,b_)-separator extending _M_.<tbc>

• _Ti_ contains all \(\alpha\)-vertices: let us fix \(S=N(C(b,\Omega))\). If _S_ contains every vertex of _M_, then again _S_ is a minimal (_a,b_)-separator extending _M_. Assume by way of contradiction that it is not the case. Component \(C(b,\Omega)\) is adjacent to all vertices in \(\{a_i,b_i\}_{1\le i\le n}\). So, \(C(b,\Omega)\) is not adjacent to some clause vertex _Cj_. Then, in the gadget where |_Ti_|=3, since we added an \(\alpha\)-vertex, vertex _bi_ is not adjacent to \(C(a,\Omega)\). Finally, as _Cj_ is not adjacent to \(C(b,\Omega)\) and \((b_i,C_j)\notin E(G(\Phi))\), then (_bi,Cj_) is a conflict pair for \(\Omega\), which yields a contradiction. In brief, the existence of a PMC \(\Omega\) extending _M_ and avoiding {_a,b_} allows us to identify a minimal (_a,b_)-separator extending _M_ in \(G(\Phi)\). The hardness of PMC Extension thus comes naturally. **Theorem 3.** PMC Extension _is NP-complete._ _Proof._ By Theorem 12, it is NP-hard to find a minimal (_a,b_)-separator extending _M_ in graphs \(G(\Phi)\).
